questions.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the head of a pin?

options.why: Chose the unit that suits a stamp or a phone screen, which are far wider than a pin head.
Chose a room-sized unit, which would make the pin head a decimal with several leading zeros.

questions.solution_text:
A pin head is about a millimetre across.
The square millimetre is the square that matches a surface that small.
$\text{mm}^2$

questions.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the state of Queensland?

options.why: Chose the unit used for paddocks, which would give a state an area running into the millions.
Chose a room-sized unit, which would give a state an area with more than twelve digits.

questions.solution_text:
Queensland stretches well over a thousand kilometres in each direction.
Only the square kilometre is large enough to give a number that can be read.
$\text{km}^2$

questions.question_text: Which of these is most likely to have an area of about $2\text{ m}^2$?

options.why: Treated a square metre as a hand-sized square rather than a square with sides one metre long.
Treated a square metre as the size of a whole playing surface instead of a single square metre.
Confused square metres with hectares, the unit that actually suits farmland.

questions.solution_text:
A square metre is about the size of a small table top, and a single bed is roughly two of them.
A bus ticket is far smaller and the court and farm are far larger.
A single bed.

questions.question_text: Which of these is most likely to have an area of about $50$ ha?

options.why: Treated a hectare as a house-sized area rather than a square $100$ m by $100$ m.
Confused hectares with square metres, the unit that suits an indoor floor.
Treated hectares as city-sized; a capital city runs to hundreds of square kilometres.

questions.solution_text:
One hectare is a square $100$ m by $100$ m, so $50$ ha is land about $700$ m by $700$ m.
That is paddock-sized: far larger than a backyard, far smaller than a city.
A large wheat paddock.

questions.question_text: Which list gives the units of area in order from smallest to largest?

options.why: Placed ha after $\text{km}^2$, assuming a hectare is larger than a square kilometre when in fact $1\text{ km}^2 = 100$ ha.
Swapped the two smallest units, treating a centimetre as shorter than a millimetre when $1$ cm $= 10$ mm.
Swapped the two smallest units and also placed ha after $\text{km}^2$, so both ends of the list are in the wrong order.

questions.solution_text:
The squares are built on sides of $1$ mm, $1$ cm, $1$ m, $100$ m and $1000$ m.
Ordering the sides orders the squares.
$\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$, ha, $\text{km}^2$

questions.question_text:
A farm's area is recorded as $250\,000\text{ m}^2$.
Which unit would present this area best?

options.why: Kept the recorded unit even though a six-digit count is hard to compare with other farms.
Jumped to the region-sized unit, giving a decimal well below $1$ for a single farm.

questions.solution_text:
A six-digit count of square metres is accurate but hard to picture.
Hectares are the unit used for farmland and turn the same area into a short whole number.
ha

questions.question_text:
Tom writes the area of his phone screen as $0.0104\text{ m}^2$.
Which unit would present this area best?

options.why: Dropped two units down the ladder, turning a hand-sized screen into a five-digit count.
Kept the recorded unit even though a screen is a decimal with two leading zeros in square metres.

questions.solution_text:
A square metre is far bigger than a phone screen, so the reading sits well below $1$.
A screen is about $10$ cm by $10$ cm, so the square centimetre gives a readable whole number.
$\text{cm}^2$

questions.question_text:
A council report records four areas: a postage stamp on a letter, a lounge-room rug, the local sports ground and the whole council area.
Which set of units is most appropriate, in that order?

options.why: Shifted every choice one unit too small, treating each item as smaller than it really is.
Kept square metres for the sports ground, giving a five-digit count for a paddock-sized area.
Jumped to square kilometres for the sports ground, giving an area far below $1$.

questions.solution_text:
A stamp is a few centimetres each way: $\text{cm}^2$.
A rug is a couple of metres each way: $\text{m}^2$.
A sports ground is hundreds of metres each way: ha.
A council area spans several kilometres: $\text{km}^2$.
Each unit is the one whose square is closest in size to the thing being measured.
